title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of Buckeye Power, Inc. to certain Comments and Protests re PJM Interconnection, LLC’s proposal to Establish Interim Resources Adequacy, et al. under ER26-3515.

documents.name: Buckeye Answer ER26-3515.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

         PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                               Docket No. ER26-3515-000




                           MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER
                         AND ANSWER OF BUCKEYE POWER, INC.

           Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s

(“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Buckeye Power, Inc. (“Buckeye”) 2

respectfully moves for leave to answer and answers certain comments and protests filed

in this proceeding (“Answer”). Buckeye seeks to provide additional information and

context that will assist the Commission in its decision-making process, particularly as it

relates to the impact of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) Interim Resource

Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) proposal on self-supply entities like Buckeye.

           On August 13, 2026, PJM submitted revisions to the PJM Open Access

Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among

Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish IRAS. 3 Numerous parties filed comments

and protests addressing the proposal, including Buckeye. 4 Several parties raised concerns

in their comments and protests about the problematic impact of the definition of “New

2

(Aug. 20, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260820-5106.

  Limited Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc. (Sep. 3, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260903-5125. As Buckeye

                                                 -2-


Large Loads” on existing loads and on Load Serving Entities like Buckeye that have

secured sufficient generation resources to serve their load, whether new or existing

(“Self-Supply LSE”). 5 Buckeye files this answer to address those comments, and to

express support for specific issues raised by East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc.

(“EKPC”), 6 the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition (“PJM ICC”), 7 and the Public

Utilities Commission of Ohio’s Office of the Federal Energy Advocate (“Ohio FEA”). 8

I.         MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

           Buckeye respectfully requests leave to answer the comments and protests filed in

the above-captioned proceeding on September 3, 2026. While the Commission’s

regulations do not permit answers to answers unless otherwise authorized by the

Commission,9 the Commission may waive this prohibition for good cause. 10 The

Commission has found good cause exists where an answer would assist its decision-

making process. 11 Good cause exists here, as Buckeye’s Answer clarifies important

issues regarding PJM’s IRAS filing.


5
  Self-Supply is defined in the PJM Tariff as “Capacity Resources secured by a [LSE], by ownership or
contract, outside a Reliability Pricing Model Auction, and used to meet obligations under this Attachment
or the [RAA] through submission in a Base Residual Auction or an Incremental Auction of a Sell Offer
indicating such Market Seller’s intent that such Capacity Resource be Self-Supply. Self-Supply may be
either committed regardless of clearing price or submitted as a Sell Offer with a price bid. A [LSE’s] Sell
Offer with a price bid for an owned or contracted Capacity Resource shall not be deemed ‘Self-Supply,’
unless it is designated as Self-Supply and used by the LSE to meet obligations under this Attachment or the
[RAA].” PJM Tariff, Definitions – Self-Supply.
6
  Limited Protest of East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc. (Sep. 3, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260903-5229
(“EKPC Limited Protest”).
7
 Comments of the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition (Sep. 3, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260903-5231 (“PJM
ICC Comments”).
8
 Comments of the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio’s Office of the Federal Energy Advocate (Sep. 3,
2026), eLibrary No. 20260903-5190 (“Ohio FEA Comments”).
9
    18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2).
10
     Id. § 385.101(e).
11
  See, e.g., Pac. Gas & Elec. Co., 183 FERC ¶ 61,159, P 18 (2023); Pac. Gas & Elec. Co., 183 FERC
¶ 61,202, P 30 (2023).

II.      ANSWER

         PJM’s IRAS is aimed at addressing resource adequacy concerns that have been

primarily driven by new data center load. 12 Data centers are not only driving the

unprecedented load growth in PJM, they also have unique characteristics that present

distinct challenges to the grid. 13 Despite the clear and specific cause of these problems,

PJM’s IRAS proposal—specifically the requirement that New Large Loads face

curtailment if they do not have Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”)—is broadly

targeted at all large loads over 50 MW. That covers new manufacturing and other

traditional industrial and commercial loads, as well as load increases of existing similar

loads that bring total load above 50 MW.

         Buckeye agrees with EKPC that this broad application of PJM’s IRAS proposal is

particularly problematic for Self-Supply LSEs, like Buckeye, that have planned for this


12
   PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 6 (“Insufficient commitments of capacity in the 2027/2028 and
2028/2029 Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) Auctions, primarily driven by the unprecedented addition of
large loads, most notably data centers, have given rise to resource adequacy shortfalls—and associated
real-time operational issues that IRAS is intended to address.” (emphasis added)); id. at 13 (“PJM hosts the
largest concentration of data center load in the world.”); id. at 21 (explaining that the capacity shortfall
facing PJM “is due to a confluence of various factors, particularly the ‘unprecedented surge in data center
load’ at a faster pace than new supply can come online, and the ‘speed of connecting these large loads
creates a fundamental misalignment between demand and supply cycles’” (footnotes omitted, quoting PJM,
2027/2028 Base Residual Auction Reserve Target Shortfall Report at 1, 4 (Feb. 9, 2026),
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2027-2028/2027-2028-bra-
reserve-target-shortfall-report.pdf [https://perma.cc/TA3Y-95AX])).
13
   See Reliability Standard(s) Pertaining to Computational Load Integration, 196 FERC ¶ 61,031, P 9
(2026) (“We agree with [North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”)] regarding the urgent
need for action to assure that computational loads are reliably integrated into the operation of the Bulk-
Power System. NERC has documented multiple grid disturbances in which computational loads have
caused or contributed to the instability of the Bulk-Power System.”) (citing NERC, Supplemental ANOPR
Comments at 1 n.1, Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large Loads, Docket No. RM26-4
(Mar. 20, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260320-5091; see also NERC, Incident Review: Considering
Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reduction s (Jan. 8, 2025), https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-
work/reports/event- reports/incident_review_large_load_loss.pdf; NERC, Incident Review: Voltage-
Sensitive Crypto Load Reductions (Jan. 9, 2026), https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-
work/reports/event-reports/incident_review_considering_voltage- sensitive_crypto_load_reductions.pdf;
see also NERC, 2026 State of Reliability: Assessment Overview of 2025 Bulk Power System Performance
at 5-6 (June 24, 2026), https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/programs/rapa/pa/
nerc_sor_2026_overview.pdf).
                                                  -4-


traditional load growth and ensured that they own or are entitled to sufficient resources to

cover this conventional load growth. It is not just and reasonable to impose IRAS

requirements on existing loads experiencing organic load growth when a Self-Supply

LSE has planned for and obtained generation to cover that same load growth

        To avoid this unjust and unreasonable outcome, Buckeye requests the

Commission clarify or direct PJM to adjust its filing to revise the definition of New Large

Loads to apply only to data centers. 14 Alternatively, the Commission should require PJM

to limit the definition of New Large Loads to only those loads that are truly new, and

exclude incremental growth of existing loads that are served by Self-Supply LSEs that

have sufficient resources to meet the demand of that load growth. At a minimum, the

Commission should adopt PJM ICC’s proposal to change the existing New Large Load

definition to only apply to existing load that has increased by 50 MW rather than

increased incrementally to over 50 MW to avoid absurd and problematic results.

        A.       Buckeye is a Self-Supply LSE.

        Buckeye, as a Self-Supply LSE, operates to ensure that it either owns or is entitled

to sufficient generation resources to cover the needs of its member-electric distribution

cooperatives and their retail members. For over 60 years, Buckeye has planned its

generation portfolio to ensure that there are sufficient generation resources to serve not

only its existing load, but organic load growth. The organic load growth Buckeye plans

for includes increased demand needs at existing loads and the addition of new

commercial and industrial facilities that would locate on its member-electric distribution



14
   For example, the Commission has directed the North American Electric Reliability Corporation to file
Reliability Standards specific to “computational loads,” recognizing the unique nature of these specific
large loads. 196 FERC ¶ 61,031, Ordering Paragraph (A).
                                                   -5-


cooperatives’ systems. As a result of this planning, Buckeye currently owns or is entitled

to generation output that exceeds its members’ current load requirements, plus reserves,

and is sufficient to meet organic load growth for many years into the future.

         Buckeye’s distribution cooperative members, and in turn their retail members,

have paid for this generation at-cost with the expectation that the generation in excess of

current load will be available to cover organic load growth for which it was planned.

Buckeye agrees with EKPC that precluding such Self-Supply LSEs from relying on these

planned resources, particularly for growth of existing traditional loads, undermines

settled expectations and is potentially not just and reasonable. 15

         To illustrate why PJM’s proposal is overly broad and not just and reasonable,

assume a Buckeye has a retail member manufacturing facility with 45 MW of current

load that has been in operation for decades, and that Buckeye has planned its generation

portfolio based on this member’s existing load and potential future growth. This member

(and others) has paid through its rates for Buckeye’s generation supply at cost for the

decades it has been in operation. This member seeks to expand its operations by adding 6

MW of load, and 100 new jobs, increasing its overall load to 51 MW—within the range

of future load growth for which Buckeye has planned and obtained generation. Despite

Buckeye having excess generation in its portfolio built and paid for by its members for

the very purpose of supplying this growth, Buckeye or the load must now go out and

build or acquire an additional 6 MW of new generation to serve this growth or be subject

to curtailment under PJM’s IRAS proposal. Faced with the cost of this proposition, the



15
  “[I]t is not just and reasonable to subject to IRAS curtailment the load of an LSE that has prudently
planned its power supply portfolio to include sufficient resources to meet its load-serving obligations,
including for New Large Load.” EKPC Comments at 15.
                                                  -6-


member may decide not to expand, sacrificing 100 new jobs. This outcome is not only

unfair, but it is also completely unnecessary to meet the resource adequacy challenges

posed by hyper-scale data centers.

           The Commission can avoid, or mitigate, this concern without losing the benefits

of PJM’s IRAS filing by narrowing the scope of the definition of New Large Load as

proposed below.

           B.       Buckeye supports limiting the definition of New Large Load to
                    data centers.

           There is no question that the large imbalance PJM is experiencing between

expected load growth and available generation resources is driven primarily by data

centers. 16 To combat this imbalance, PJM is proposing IRAS as an operational tool to

address the reality that data centers are seeking to interconnect to the electric grid more

quickly than generation and transmission can be built, making it difficult for PJM to

maintain a reliable electric grid. 17 But as the Ohio FEA recognized in its filing, PJM’s

IRAS filing makes no distinction “between the computational loads that are directly

responsible for the current state of resource adequacy—such as hyperscale data centers

and cryptocurrency miners—and traditional manufacturing loads that drive American

industry.” 18

           Despite data centers driving the need for IRAS, PJM has defined “New Large

Loads” broadly to include traditional loads, both new and existing: 19


16
     See supra note 12.
17
  PJM Filing, Attach. C, Affidavit of Christopher Pilong on Behalf of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., P 19
(“Pilong Aff.”).
18
     Ohio FEA Comments at 4.
19
   PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 38 (quoting id. Attach. A, Redline Tariff, Definitions – New Large
Load at 46).
                                                     -7-


                    “New Large Load” means “an end-use customer load that is
                    either (a) a Large Load that goes into service after June 1,
                    2027, or (b) incremental load in-service after June 1, 2027,
                    that increases the existing end-use customer load at a single
                    electrical site that, prior to such incremental load, did not
                    previously meet the definition of Large Load.”

PJM’s proposed definition of “Large Load,” incorporated into the term “New Large

Load,” is: 20

                    end-use customer(s) load that has a cumulative peak load of
                    50 megawatts or greater at a single electrical site behind one
                    or more points of interconnection, where for configurations
                    involving multiple affiliated load facilities or multiple points
                    of interconnection with affiliated load facilities behind them,
                    all affiliated load facilities within a one-mile radius will be
                    considered a single electrical site as further described in the
                    PJM Manuals.

           Buckeye agrees with the Ohio FEA that revising the definition of New Large

Load to apply solely to data centers would better align PJM’s IRAS proposal with the

underlying cause of the resource adequacy concerns it seeks to address. 21 Indeed, it is

well established that treating differently situated entities the same constitutes undue

discrimination under the Federal Power Act. 22 Applying IRAS only to data centers would

also ensure that the generation resource portfolio that Buckeye (and other Self-Supply

LSEs) has built over decades to serve its existing load, plus organic load growth of

existing load and the potential for new traditional loads, remains preserved.

           PJM has consented to the Commission modifying its filing “where such

modification is consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives in this filing.” 23 Limiting


20
     Id. at 31 (quoting id. Attach. A, Redline Tariff, Definitions – New Large Load at 123).
21
  Ohio FEA Comments at 4-5. As the Ohio FEA notes, this is the approach that all investor-owned utilities
in Ohio have taken so far.
22
     Ala. Elec. Coop., Inc. v. FERC, 684 F.2d 20, 27 (D.C. Cir. 1982).
23
     PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 122.
                                           -8-


the scope of New Large Loads to data centers would be consistent with the purpose of

IRAS because the data center loads that are driving the resource adequacy concerns

would still be subject to BYONC or curtailment.

       C.      In the alternative, Buckeye supports removing existing loads
               served by Self-Supply LSEs from the definition of New Large
               Loads.

       If the Commission does not limit the definition of New Large Loads to data center

loads, Buckeye alternatively supports removing from the definition of New Large Load

existing loads that are served by Self-Supply LSEs with sufficient generation resources in

their portfolios. As noted above, Self-Supply LSEs have planned their generation

portfolios to provide generation supply to their existing loads along with organic load

growth. These Self-Supply LSEs, and their customers, have paid for this generation

portfolio with the expectation that excess generation will be available to cover future

growth.

       It is not just and reasonable for PJM to now require Self-Supply LSEs, and in turn

the loads they serve, to either be subject to curtailment or bear the cost of building new

generation capacity for existing loads that expand over 50 MW. Establishing a narrowly

tailored exception to the scope of New Large Loads for Self-Supply LSEs with sufficient

excess generation available to support expansion of existing loads would avoid this

problem. Similar to the discussion above, this modification of PJM’s proposal would be

consistent with IRAS’s overall objectives, since it would still require data centers that are

causing the resource adequacy problems identified by PJM to be subject to either

BYONC or curtailment.
                                             -9-


           D.     At a minimum, the Commission should adopt PJM ICC’s
                  proposal to apply New Large Loads only to existing loads than
                  increase by 50 MW or more.

           The Commission should, at a minimum, adopt the PJM ICC’s proposal that the

definition of New Large Load apply only to existing loads that increase by an increment

of 50 MW, rather than existing loads that increase to over 50 MW. As proposed by PJM

ICC: “When an existing Large Load facility expands, only load growth over 50 MW

from the baseline should be subject to IRAS. (That is, a 50 MW facility should not be

subjected to IRAS until it expands beyond 100 MW.)” 24

           This clarification would avoid the absurd result described above where an existing

manufacturing load can increase its load by 6 MW (or less) and be subject to curtailment

or be required to pay to bring 6 MW of new generation to the market. In addition,

requiring BYONC for small, incremental load increases may be infeasible in many

instances, given the lumpy nature of new capacity. This change would not undermine the

purpose of IRAS and the resource adequacy concerns it is intended to address. As noted

by PJM ICC, “[m]any of the new computational loads are significantly in excess of

50 MW, whereas 50 MW is not unusual for an industrial or institutional facility.” 25

III.       CONCLUSION

           To the extent PJM does not address the issues described above on its own,

Buckeye requests the Commission direct PJM to (i) revise the definition of New Large

Loads to apply only to data centers, or, in the alternative; (ii) limit the definition of New

Large Loads only to loads that are truly new, and exclude incremental growth of existing



24
     PJM ICC Comments at 4.
25
     Id.
                                                  - 10 -


loads that are served by Self-Supply LSEs that have sufficient resources to meet the

demand of the load. At a minimum, the Commission should adopt PJM ICC’s proposal to

change the existing New Large Load definition only to only apply to existing load that

has increased by 50 MW rather than increased to over 50 MW.

           As described above, each of these changes would be “consistent with PJM’s

overarching objectives in this filing.” 26 They likewise would not result in an entirely

different rate design than what PJM has proposed, 27 as the core elements of PJM’s IRAS

proposal would be retained and still apply to the data centers causing the resource

adequacy issues IRAS is intended to address.
